title: Matroids / linear algebra over F₂: the 'sign vectors' of divisors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^×/squares
connection: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo squares is an F₂-vector space; prime factors of 4Cp+1 give vectors; −1 is a target vector; subset-product hits −1 in the quotient iff −1 ∈ span (a linear algebra question!). The full condition (−1 as a subset product, not mod squares) is harder, but the F₂-relaxation is linear and decidable by rank.
why: The F₂-relaxation is a necessary condition for a win that is *linear* — and its failure probability is exactly 2^{−(rank deficiency)}; it isolates the 'genus-like' part (characters of order 2) from the rest. Repo's 'genus layer is pointwise free' lemma may be this.
first_step: git grep -il 'genus layer' -- '*.md' and compare; then compute for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 100: does the F₂-relaxation hold (−1 ∈ span of factor vectors mod squares) and how often does the full condition fail when the relaxation holds?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Catalog: Gaussian primes in narrow sectors / Hecke Größencharaktere
connection: Gaussian primes in narrow sectors / Hecke Größencharaktere ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: none. Status: proved for sectors of power width. Mechanism: Hecke L-functions.
why: Angular equidistribution — ES Gaussian liftings would need sector control.

title: Divisor equations in the Erdős–Straus parametrisation
connection: The divisor-sum formulation shares F10, F15, F21, F29: an ES witness exists iff a p-tied integer has a divisor in a prescribed residue class (this sub-problem is open, not solved).
why: Techniques for residue-restricted divisors may provide a pointwise lower bound in the hard splitting case.
first_step: For prime p≡1 mod 4, derive the precise divisor interval and compare with known bounds for divisors in arithmetic progressions.

title: Connection: correlation between families measured by survivor statistics
connection: In the residue model, families are independent if δ(X) equals ∏(1 − density of family). Comparing the observed δ(X) with the independent product quantifies correlation exactly (no primes needed).
why: Correlation is the one unknown dividing-line coordinate for ES; this is a direct, cheap measurement.
first_step: Compute ∏_{families ≤ X}(1 − |res|/φ(m)·…) (careful with non-unit residues) vs observed δ(X).

title: One-parameter form: R(p) = #{m ≡ 3 (mod 4) : r_p(m) | (m+1)/4}, r_p(m) = (−p mod m) (CHECKED p ≤ 1009)
connection: Trial form (4uC−1) | p+u with m = 4uC−1 forces u = r_p(m) (as 1 ≤ u < m), so R(p) counts moduli m ≡ 3 mod 4 whose ceiling-remainder divides (m+1)/4 ↔ a single-variable search over m.
why: A one-variable reformulation makes 'remainder of one integer modulo a running modulus' the whole problem — the classical object of the Dirichlet divisor problem and of p mod m statistics (Vinogradov), possibly opening Voronoi/exponential-sum tools.
first_step: Verified numerically (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check1.py, p ≤ 1009 incl. 409 → 0). Next: plot r_p(m)/m against m for hard p and study the arcs where r_p(m) is small (m just above p/q).

title: Problem 314: extremal reciprocal bounds and Poisson scale
connection: Problem 314 ↔ ES F04, F12, F24, F37: representation-scale heuristic, reciprocal extremals and count fluctuations.
why: The page discusses a conjectured best exponent; its extremal examples may help calibrate tails in the ES witness-count heuristic.
first_step: Inspect the examples attaining the lower bound and compare their reciprocal-sum multiplicities with the predicted log-scale distribution of R(p).

title: ES in 'Z with a different order': positive cone = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 4 or …} is not multiplicatively closed — design check
connection: Orders on Z other than the usual one don't exist (Z has a unique ordering as an ordered ring). So 'other positivity on Z' must be a semigroup restriction (constraint worlds), not a new order.
why: Closes a tempting but empty direction; constraint worlds (batch C) cover the meaningful variants.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Shift two unit fractions while preserving exactness
connection: The Egyptian-fraction rewriting operator in arXiv:2003.13229 and ES F12/F14/F27: exact reciprocal decompositions admit local transformations while positivity/parity constrain the result.
why: A local rewrite may move a representation into the denominator congruence classes required by ES without changing the sum.
first_step: Read the operator identity and apply it to a two-term portion of a known three-term ES identity; check whether it preserves three terms and positivity.

title: Counting distinct unit-fraction solutions, not just proving existence
connection: MathOverflow 229514 asks for the number of strictly increasing tuples with reciprocal sum 1 and reports the unique 3-term solution 1/2+1/3+1/6. This shares F04/F12/F14/F21: an exact representation-count problem with symmetry removed and pointwise counts rather than existence alone.
why: A canonical count framework can clarify what ES's R(p) should count (ordered, unordered, or distinct denominators) and how symmetries affect estimates.
first_step: Adopt the increasing-denominator convention from the MO question and recompute small-prime ES representation counts, comparing them to ordered counts after dividing by S3 orbit sizes.

title: Which composites fail the C-form? Test whether C-form exceptions are closed under multiplication by squares or by other exceptions
connection: If n fails the C-form, does n·m² fail? (T1-like scaling: for squares the obstruction is via (a/m²) = 1; for n·m²: (a/nm²) = (a/n) — so the QNR condition reduces to that of n; and 4C·nm² + 1 = ab with a ≡ −1 (4C) — different integer.) Empirically test closure properties of the exceptional set E = {n : no C-form certificate}.
why: Structural properties of E (closure, multiplicativity) constrain any eventual characterisation; e.g. if E ⊇ {odd squares} ∪ {409 m² : m odd}, there are infinite non-square families, changing the 'squares + sporadic' expectation for this sub-conjecture.

title: Reorganise search: 'barrier-first' dataset of every approach × which step fails, as a public table
connection: Repo's barriers B1–B9 ↔ a public, structured negative-results database prevents others from repeating.
why: Negative results are under-published; a curated table is a community service and clarifies what remains.
first_step: Export FRONTIER §3/§4 barrier map as a CSV with (approach, step, barrier, reference) and render as a web page.

title: Carmichael numbers are ES-rich, not ES-hard: U(n) is 3.3–5.7× the neighbour median
why: Although n ≡ 1 modulo each p−1 (the 'hard' congruence shape), having ≥ 3 prime factors multiplies divisor structure; the p ≡ 1 (mod L) hardness mechanism does not survive multiplicatively — hardness is a prime phenomenon.
first_step: Compare with semiprimes pq where both p, q are ES-hard (e.g. 193·241) to see whether hardness compounds at all.

title: Logarithmic geometry of denominator exclusions
connection: Treat denominator vanishing loci as a marked divisor and compare charts respecting that divisor.
why: A log-geometric description may organize which coordinate changes preserve the relevant open set.
first_step: Write the marked boundary for two birational charts and compute how each boundary factor transforms.

title: Chinese remainder optimization
connection: Treat parameter selection as a CRT problem with a cost function on the resulting least positive representative.
why: Congruence compatibility and parameter size are distinct, computable parts of certificate design.
first_step: Combine three small valid congruence conditions and optimize the CRT representative by varying their residues.
